title: Effective Hardcore Exclusion Without Exclusion: Two-Species Pair Annihilation Revisited
abstract: Reaction-diffusion systems with two species that mutually annihilate through $A+B\to\emptyset$ reactions display a slow decay of the total density $ρ$ which follows an anomalous power law in low dimensions. For hardcore particles in one dimension, this decay follows $ρ\sim t^{-1/4}$ under symmetric diffusion and $ρ\sim t^{-1/3}$ under asymmetric diffusion without relative bias between the two species. The $t^{-1/3}$ behavior, in particular, has so far been observed exclusively in systems with hardcore exclusion. Here we construct a model of particles without hardcore exclusion that reproduces this same $t^{-1/3}$ scaling. In our model, both species undergo asymmetric diffusion with a rate that depends nonlinearly on the local density, a form of transport that, in the absence of the other species, is superdiffusive and falls into the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang universality class. The scaling behavior of $t^{-1/3}$ occurs when at least one of the two species undergoes asymmetric diffusion induced by microscopic processes involving pairs of particles, while asymmetric processes involving groups of three particles lead to $t^{-1/4}$ scaling associated with symmetric diffusion. This demonstrates that the pair annihilation density decay exponent is not determined exclusively by the transport properties of the isolated particle species.
summary: This paper theoretically analyzes the density decay in two-species pair annihilation systems, showing that the resulting anomalous power-law decay exponent is not solely dictated by the diffusion mechanism of the individual species. By constructing a bosonic model, the authors successfully reproduce the $t^{-1/3}$ scaling previously thought unique to hardcore exclusion models, demonstrating the profound influence of pair interactions on non-equilibrium dynamics.
main_problem: The paper investigates the density decay exponent in reaction-diffusion systems with two mutually annihilating species ($A+B 	o \emptyset$), comparing results from hardcore exclusion models to bosonic models.
main_result: The pair annihilation density decay exponent ($\delta$) is not determined exclusively by the transport properties of the isolated species; the $t^{-1/3}$ scaling can be reproduced in a bosonic model, contrasting with $t^{-1/4}$ scaling from three-body hopping.
method: The analysis uses the Doi-Peliti formalism to map the discrete master equation to a continuum field theory, analyzing scaling behavior using the Family-Vicsek relation and Renormalization Group techniques.
model_or_system: The system is a 1D lattice model of two species undergoing pair annihilation ($A+B 	o \emptyset$). The dynamics are studied using a bosonic framework, allowing for nonlinear hopping rates dependent on local density.
key_observables: Total density decay exponent ($\delta$), dynamic exponent ($z$), and the width scaling function $w(L, t)$.
important_parameters: The type of hopping process (two-body vs. three-body) and the presence/absence of relative bias in diffusion rates.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on mapping the discrete dynamics to a continuum field theory and assuming the validity of scaling hypotheses (e.g., KPZ or EW universality classes).
figures_summary: Figures demonstrate scaling collapse for both EW ($\alpha=1/2, z=2$) and KPZ ($ eta=1/3, z=3/2$) regimes, confirming the predicted exponents for different hopping mechanisms.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the general framework using the Doi-Peliti formalism, analyzing the single-species case (mapping to surface growth/Burgers' equation), and finally applying this to the two-species pair annihilation problem to compare different nonlinear hopping terms.
why_interesting: The work provides a deep theoretical understanding of how microscopic interaction rules (like pair vs. three-body hopping) dictate macroscopic universal scaling exponents in non-equilibrium statistical physics, which is crucial for understanding complex many-body dynamics.
